def-ca.summary: Calcium moves poorly inside the plant, so symptoms appear on fruit and new leaves, e.g. tomato blossom-end rot and cabbage tipburn.
symptoms: New tissue is affected first (calcium moves poorly).
On tomato and sweet pepper, the blossom end of the fruit first looks water-soaked, then turns dark brown and sunken (blossom-end rot).
Inner leaf margins of cabbage, Chinese cabbage and lettuce turn brown and scorched (heart rot, tipburn).
Growing points shrivel.
def-ca.conditions: A lack of calcium in the soil is often not the main cause. More often it is uneven water supply (big swings between wet and dry), fast transpiration in hot weather, or excess ammonium nitrogen or potassium competing with calcium, so calcium cannot reach the fruit and inner leaves. Root damage can also cause it.
prevention: Keep soil moisture steady (mulching, drip irrigation).
Apply lime to acidic soils.
Avoid over-applying ammonium nitrogen and potassium fertilizer.
In greenhouses, ventilate well and manage temperature and humidity.
control: At early fruit enlargement, spray a calcium product (e.g. calcium chloride, calcium nitrate) on the leaves and onto the fruit; watch the concentration to avoid spray injury.
Remove affected fruit.

illus.cap: Dark brown sunken blossom end on tomato (blossom-end rot)
Inner leaf margins scorched (tipburn)

cropNotes.tomato: Blossom-end rot: a water-soaked, brownish black sunken patch at the fruit tip (where the flower fell); common in drought or with uneven watering.
cropNotes.pepper: Grayish white to brown sunken dry patches on the lower half or side of the fruit (blossom-end rot); common in hot, dry periods.
cropNotes.crucifer: Inner leaf margins of heading Chinese cabbage and cabbage turn brown and scorched (heart rot, tipburn); the head looks normal outside and the damage only shows when cut open.
cropNotes.cucurbit: Sunken black rot at the blossom end of watermelon and other fruit (blossom-end rot); new leaf margins dry and curl.
cropNotes.potato: Brown spots or hollows inside tubers; terminal buds die.
cropNotes.strawberry: New leaf tips scorched and crinkled (tipburn), sepal tips turn brown; common in hot weather with high transpiration, or when humidity is too high.
cropNotes.mango: Flesh at the fruit tip softens early and looks water-soaked (soft nose), linked to low calcium in the fruit.
cropNotes.goldenberry: Fruit cracks easily, new leaves curl and growing points are damaged; more obvious when soil moisture swings sharply.

def-fe.name: Iron (Fe) deficiency
def-fe.summary: Common in alkaline soils. New leaves turn yellowish white between the veins while the veins stay green in a fine net.
symptoms: New leaves yellow between the veins first; veins stay green in a fine net pattern.
In severe cases whole new leaves turn yellowish white.
Old leaves are usually normal.
def-fe.conditions: Iron is poorly soluble in alkaline or calcareous soils (pH above about 7.5). It also occurs with poor drainage, excess phosphate fertilizer or too much manganese. Common in citrus, blueberry and others.
prevention: Correct soil pH (e.g. apply sulfur powder or acidic organic matter).
Improve drainage.
Use alkaline-tolerant rootstocks.
control: Spray chelated iron (e.g. Fe-EDTA) on the leaves several times in a row.
For soil application in alkaline soils, use Fe-EDDHA.

illus.cap: New leaves yellowish white between veins, fine green net
Starts on upper, new leaves

cropNotes.rice: Seedlings in upland fields or alkaline soils: new leaves yellowish white and striped, growth stops.
cropNotes.strawberry: New leaves yellowish white with green veins; common when soil is alkaline, too wet or poorly drained.
cropNotes.citrus: New leaves yellowish white between the veins with a green vein network; most common on alkaline or calcareous soils.
cropNotes.grape: On calcareous soils, leaves on new shoots turn yellowish white; in severe cases leaf margins scorch and clusters develop poorly.
cropNotes.mango: Leaves on new shoots turn yellowish white; more common on alkaline soils or when roots are damaged.

def-b.name: Boron (B) deficiency
def-b.summary: Growing points and reproductive organs are hit first, causing hollow stems, flower drop, cracked fruit and misshapen fruit.
symptoms: Growing points shrivel and die; new leaves are misshapen, thick and brittle.
Cauliflower and cabbage stems turn hollow and brown inside (hollow stem); radish gets brown heart.
Flower drop and poor fruit set.
Fruit cracks and is misshapen (e.g. bumpy papaya fruit, hardened citrus peel).
def-b.conditions: Deficiency is common in sandy soils, after heavy rain leaches the soil, or in drought; heavy liming that raises pH can also cause it.
prevention: Apply a moderate amount of borax or borate in the basal dressing.
Caution: the safe range for boron is very narrow, and too much easily causes toxicity.
control: Spray boric acid or borax on the leaves around flowering (about 0.1-0.2%).
Never over-apply.

illus.cap: Growing point shrivels and dies
Fruit cracked and misshapen

cropNotes.corn: Ears poorly filled, with missing kernels or irregular rows on the cob.
cropNotes.tomato: Growing point dies, internodes shorten; fruit surface cracks or turns corky.
cropNotes.crucifer: Cauliflower curds turn brown and stems are hollow (hollow stem); radish roots have brown heart inside.
cropNotes.strawberry: New leaves crinkled and misshapen, leaf tips scorched; fruit small and misshapen with few seeds.
cropNotes.citrus: Peel thickens and hardens, fruit misshapen, gummy brown spots in the peel and core.
cropNotes.grape: Poor berry set, berries of mixed sizes in the same cluster (hens and chicks); short internodes on new shoots.
cropNotes.papaya: Fruit surface bumpy and lumpy, often with hard lumps of congealed latex in the flesh; fruit drops easily.
cropNotes.goldenberry: More cracked and misshapen fruit; shoot growing points die back and internodes shorten.
cropNotes.coconut: New fronds emerge with leaflets stuck together, crumpled or hooked ("hook leaf"); severe cases deform the spear leaf and reduce nut set.

def-zn.name: Zinc (Zn) deficiency
def-zn.summary: New leaves are small and narrow, internodes short and clustered (little leaf), with mottled yellowing between the veins.
symptoms: New leaves are small and narrow, internodes short, growing in clusters (little leaf, rosette).
Mottled yellowing between the veins.
Corn shows broad white bands at the base of new leaves (white bud).
Citrus leaves show yellow-green mottling; zinc deficiency mottling is symmetrical on both sides of the midrib, unlike the asymmetrical mottling of citrus greening (HLB).
def-zn.conditions: Common in alkaline soils, with heavy phosphate fertilizer use (phosphorus competes with zinc), where topsoil has eroded, and in cold weather.
prevention: Avoid over-applying phosphate fertilizer.
Apply zinc sulfate in the basal dressing.
control: Spray zinc sulfate (about 0.2-0.5%) or chelated zinc on the leaves.

illus.cap: Small new leaves, short internodes, clustered growth
Mottled yellowing between veins (symmetrical)

cropNotes.rice: 2-4 weeks after transplanting, brown spots appear on lower leaves, plants are stunted and tillering stops (commonly called rice leaf-shrink).
cropNotes.corn: Broad white to pale yellow stripes on both sides of the base of new leaves on young plants (white bud); short internodes.
cropNotes.citrus: Leaves on new shoots small and pointed, mottled yellow between the veins (little leaf); short internodes, bunched twigs.
cropNotes.mango: New shoots with clusters of small leaves, short internodes; leaves small and thick.

def-mn.name: Manganese (Mn) deficiency
def-mn.summary: New or middle leaves turn pale yellow between the veins, with green bands kept along the veins and blurry edges.
symptoms: New or middle leaves turn pale yellow between the veins; veins and bands along both sides stay green.
The edges of the mottling are less sharp than with iron deficiency.
Sometimes tiny brown dead spots appear.
def-mn.conditions: Common in alkaline soils, soils with too much organic matter, and after over-liming.
prevention: Avoid over-applying lime.
Keep soil pH in a suitable range.
control: Spray manganese sulfate on the leaves (about 0.2-0.3%).

illus.cap: Pale yellow between veins, green bands along veins

cropNotes.citrus: New leaves pale green between the veins, with wider dark green bands along both sides of the veins; yellowing is milder than with iron deficiency.

def-s.name: Sulfur (S) deficiency
def-s.summary: New leaves turn evenly yellow and look like nitrogen deficiency, but nitrogen deficiency starts on old leaves while sulfur deficiency starts on new leaves.
symptoms: New leaves turn evenly yellow first (veins included).
Looks like nitrogen deficiency, but nitrogen deficiency appears on old leaves first.
Plants are stunted.
Crucifers and onion/garlic crops need a lot of sulfur and show it more easily.
def-s.conditions: Deficiency is common in sandy soils and soils low in organic matter; long-term use of only high-analysis chemical fertilizers that contain no sulfur can also cause it.
prevention: Use sulfur-containing fertilizers such as ammonium sulfate, potassium sulfate or gypsum.
Add more organic matter.
control: Top-dress with ammonium sulfate or potassium sulfate.

illus.cap: New leaves evenly yellow
Starts on upper, new leaves

cropNotes.rice: Whole plant pale yellow, more obvious on new leaves; similar to nitrogen deficiency but new leaves yellow first.
cropNotes.crucifer: Crucifers need a lot of sulfur; when deficient, new leaves yellow and get smaller, and leaf undersides may turn purplish red.
cropNotes.corn: New leaves pale yellow with stripes; plants grow slowly.
